transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Morning everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off — uh — quick agenda: usage, costs, reliability and then next steps.
[00:12] Anika Rao: Yeah thanks, Maya. We had a big spike in May — about 3x on the classification pipeline — so cost is front of mind.
[00:25] Diego Morales: Got it. Is that spike sustained or a few bursts?
[00:30] Jon Summers: Mostly sustained for two weeks, plus regular nightly batch embeddings. The embeddings are the big line-item.
[00:40] Maya Chen: Right, embeddings + long sequences drive token spend. We wanted to review batching, prefix caching, and Dedicated windows.
[00:55] Anika Rao: Curious about batching — we've tried larger batches ourselves but saw latency tail increase. How does Redwood handle tail-latency with batching?
[01:10] Diego Morales: Good question. We do continuous batching with adaptive latency SLOs — requests are routed to the fast-path when latency budget is tight, and to batched workers when throughput is priority. There's an automatic switch based on the sequence length distribution.
[01:28] Priya Desai: Can you quantify expected latency increase for 2x batching on our average payload (~1.2k tokens)?
[01:36] Diego Morales: From our benchmarks on similar models, p50 stays close, p95 can rise 20-40% depending on GPU type. But with profile-based kernel selection and KV caching for repeated prefixes you often see token-cost reduction without p95 degradation.
[01:56] Jon Summers: We also need to talk about retention. Our compliance team wants 90 day logs and customer-owned KMS.
[02:04] Maya Chen: For Private (VPC/on-prem) we support customer KMS + audit logs. Hosted can integrate KMS for key wrapping and we can retain logs to a supplied S3 — we have SOC2 artifacts that cover retention patterns.
[02:20] Priya Desai: Is that SOC2 Type II or Type I?
[02:24] Maya Chen: Type II — I'll send the whitepaper.
[02:28] Anika Rao: Thanks — please add the SOC2 contact.
[02:32] Diego Morales: From an ops perspective, if you anticipate the 3x sustained, Dedicated reserved capacity is often cheaper for heavy steady load. For spikes we recommend a Reserved base plus burst buffer or on-demand Hosted fallbacks.
[02:48] Jon Summers: Do we need Dedicated to get predictable p95?
[02:51] Diego Morales: Dedicated lowers noisy neighbor variance and lets you pin quantization and kernel config to get consistent p95. But it's a commitment. We can simulate it with a short pilot to show improvements.
[03:06] Anika Rao: What's the typical commit size for Dedicated?
[03:09] Maya Chen: It varies — many teams start with a 3-month reserved pool sized for expected steady throughput and allow autoscale for bursts. We'll share scenarios.
[03:18] Priya Desai: About encryption at rest — if we use Private VPC, are logs stored within our account?
[03:25] Maya Chen: For Private deployments we can write logs to your S3/GCS and integrate with your KMS. Hosted by default stores logs in our audit pipeline but we can export.
[03:34] Jon Summers: Can we get a cost estimate that includes embeddings, text gen, and reranking? Our product team wants per-feature line items.
[03:41] Maya Chen: Yes — Diego will produce a breakdown. We'll need your usage mix and token estimates.
[03:48] Diego Morales: Also want to highlight model variants — you can route low-criticality requests to smaller quantized variants to save costs. Some accuracy tradeoffs, but often fine for rerank or short responses.
[04:02] Anika Rao: Hmm, quantized models — how do we measure regression risk?
[04:06] Diego Morales: We suggest an eval set of 200 representative prompts, run pairwise A/B runs and we provide nlg metrics plus manual spot checks.
[04:15] Anika Rao: We'll send prompts.
[04:17] Jon Summers: We had an incident last month — long cold-start times during a midnight batch — can you explain cold-start behavior?
[04:24] Diego Morales: Cold-starts happen when KV cache and model weights aren't warm; for batched GPU pools, warm-workers and preloading reduce cold-start across a burst window. There's also a warm-cache policy to keep a light footprint replica for low-latency requests.
[04:38] Priya Desai: On the audit side, we need to record who accessed what model and when. Is per-token provenance available?
[04:45] Maya Chen: We log request metadata, model version, and user token id. Full per-token provenance is heavy, but we keep request/response with hashes for traceability.
[04:55] Anika Rao: Regarding next steps — we want that cost spreadsheet and a perf run in our staging VPC.
[05:03] Maya Chen: We'll set that up. Diego, can you coordinate the perf window?
[05:06] Diego Morales: Yep, Diego to coordinate. I'll need IAM role details and a staging S3 endpoint.
[05:11] Jon Summers: I'll confirm traffic forecasts — expect update by Monday.
[05:15] Anika Rao: We'll also share the eval prompts.
[05:18] Maya Chen: Great — recap next steps after the call. Any final questions?
[05:24] Priya Desai: One thing — can you share recommended RBAC mappings for a 3-team org (prod, infra, data science)?
[05:31] Diego Morales: Yes — standard mapping: infra = deploy+ops, data science = model/experiment, prod = limited inference and view-only for cost dashboards. We'll include a template.
[05:43] Jon Summers: Also curious on competitor differences — how much better is Redwood's routing vs Vertex AI?
[05:48] Diego Morales: Routing is more opinionated for LLM patterns: model variant fallbacks, KV-aware routing, and explicit cache policies. Vertex AI has managed endpoints but less built-in KV cache awareness for repeated-prefix workloads. (small laugh)
[06:04] Anika Rao: Okay, that makes sense.
[06:08] Maya Chen: Closing notes: Redwood will send cost model, SOC2 docs, RBAC template, and schedule VPC perf test. TidalWave will send prompts and traffic forecast. We'll reconvene after perf test.
[06:22] Jon Summers: Thanks everyone.
[06:24] Maya Chen: Thanks, talk soon.
[06:28] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional mis-attributions and typical speech disfluencies remain in the auto-transcript. Some model/product names maybe transcribed slightly off.
